text: Come by water, the way everyone has always come.
There is no road to the city, there never was.
You slip between walls of black stone down a corridor of seawater
and the walls keep coming,
eyelid after eyelid, nearly a hundred of them,
a whole capital floating on a coral reef in the middle of the Pacific.
This is Nan Madal.
Its name means within the intervals, the spaces between.
The city is the spaces, streets of seawater,
doorways that open onto the tide.
Look at the walls.
They are built of stone logs, long hexagonal columns of basalt,
formed when lava cooled a million years ago.
Layed the way you would stack firewood,
one course lengthwise, the next crosswise,
locked to the corners, no mortar, nothing but weight and patience.
Some of these stones weigh many tons.
The walls rise eight meters.
The great mortuary enclosure where the chief sleep rises 20.
And the people who raised them had no metal tools, no wheels,
no police, no draft animals, only hands and canoes and time.
The teachers asked you to sit with that for a moment,
not to solve it, to feel the size of it.
Nearly a million tons of stone,
quarried for volcanic plug on the far side of the island,
carried kilometers across the water and set here,
course upon course in the tidal zone,
where the sea itself tries twice a day to take it back.
Whatever moved those stones, it was not convenience.
It was conviction.
The islanders have their own account,
and it is worth hearing as they tell it.
Two brothers came by canoe from a western land,
twins taller than the native people,
sorcerers.
They sought a place to honor the god of the harvest,
and they found this reef.
And with rights and a flying dragon,
the old stories say they lifted the basalt through the air
and set it down in walls.
When the elder brother died of old age,
the younger became the first of the Souda-Ler kings.
The guides do not ask you to believe the dragon literally.
They ask you to notice what the story is really saying,
that the people who remember this place know in their bones,
that ordinary explanations do not suffice.
Every culture keeps one story for the thing it cannot account for.
This is theirs.
For four centuries, the Souda-Ler is ruled from this reef.
The first government to unite the island,
tribute flowing in by boat,
chiefs and priests living behind walls of stone,
while the common people lived on the main island.
It was power made visible,
a capital with no fields and no fresh water,
everything at eight and drank delivered by subjects.
And the teachers point to this gently
because it is the oldest pattern in the book.
Centralize the wonder.
Isolate the rulers, feed the machine with tribute.
Then one day a hero comes with three hundred warriors
and the pattern breaks and the city begins the long quiet of abandonment.
There is something else here,
fainter, that the guides want you to feel.
You are floating in the Pacific,
the ocean of Mu.
Long before these canals were dredged,
the old stories tell of a drowned continent in these same waters,
and of survivors who scatter to the far shores.
No one claims these stones are theirs.
The archaeology dates the great walls to less than a thousand years ago.
But stand here at dawn with the mist on the canals
and you may feel what the teachers mean when they say
the traces of earlier worlds are still among us,
asking to be contemplated.
The ocean keeps more than one memory.
So ask the question the stones are asking.
What does it take for a people to raise a city from the sea?
Vision larger than a lifetime.
Labor beyond counting.
A reason strong enough to move a million tons of rock.
And then ask the harder one.
What does it cost to keep it?
The South alurs learn the answer.
Every tribute system is a tide.
It comes in, it goes out.
The canals still run with the tide twice a day as they always have.
The stones never left.
Walk, no, drift, among the eyelids,
and let the water set the pace.
This was never a city you conquer.
It was always a city you approach slowly,
by boat, between walls of black stone.
The way everyone has always come.
It is still waiting, not for rulers, for witnesses.
